title: Pharmaceutical Analysis and Quality Control
description: Titrimetric, spectroscopic and chromatographic methods, method validation, pharmacopoeial tests, and detection of substandard and falsified medicines.

topics.title: Titrimetric Methods
topics.summary: Acid–base, non-aqueous, redox, complexometric and precipitation titrations.

notes.b: Titrimetric (volumetric) analysis measures the volume of a standard solution that reacts completely with the analyte. Primary standards (e.g. potassium hydrogen phthalate, sodium carbonate) are pure, stable and used to standardise titrants. Acid–base titrations use indicators whose colour change matches the equivalence point pH: phenolphthalein (pH 8.2–10; weak acid vs strong base), methyl orange (pH 3.1–4.4; strong acid vs weak base). Redox titrations: potassium permanganate (self-indicating, in acid), iodometry and iodimetry (starch indicator — e.g. assay of ascorbic acid), ceric sulphate. Complexometric titration with EDTA (disodium edetate) determines metal ions (calcium, magnesium, zinc) using metallochromic indicators such as Eriochrome Black T. Precipitation titrations (argentometry — silver nitrate for chlorides: Mohr, Volhard, Fajans methods).

Weakly basic or acidic drugs that give poor end points in water are titrated in non-aqueous solvents. Weak bases (many amine drugs, e.g. alkaloids, antihistamines) are titrated with perchloric acid in glacial acetic acid (a levelling solvent that enhances basicity), using crystal violet indicator or potentiometric end point; halide salts require mercuric acetate (now avoided because of toxicity) or alternative approaches. Weak acids (e.g. phenobarbital) are titrated with sodium methoxide or tetrabutylammonium hydroxide in dimethylformamide. Water must be excluded. The Karl Fischer titration determines water content in drugs and excipients.
k: Weak bases: perchloric acid in glacial acetic acid
Weak acids: sodium methoxide in DMF

topics.title: UV–Visible and Infrared Spectroscopy
topics.summary: Beer–Lambert law, UV assays, IR identification and other spectroscopic methods.

notes.b: UV–visible spectrophotometry measures absorption of 200–800 nm radiation by chromophores (conjugated systems, aromatic rings). The Beer–Lambert law: A = εcl (or A = A(1%, 1 cm) × c × l, the specific absorbance used in pharmacopoeias). Quantitative assay compares sample absorbance with a reference standard or uses the specific absorbance at λmax. Deviations from linearity occur at high concentrations, with stray light and chemical changes (e.g. pH-dependent ionisation). Instrument checks include wavelength accuracy (holmium oxide filter), absorbance accuracy (potassium dichromate) and stray light (potassium chloride). Colorimetric methods add a reagent to form a coloured product for drugs lacking a strong chromophore.

Infrared spectroscopy (4,000–400 cm⁻¹) measures molecular vibrations; the fingerprint region (below about 1,500 cm⁻¹) is unique to each compound, making IR the main pharmacopoeial identification test (comparison with a reference spectrum). Characteristic bands: O–H stretch (broad ~3,300 cm⁻¹), N–H (~3,300–3,500), C=O (~1,700 cm⁻¹), C–H (~2,900). Samples are prepared as KBr discs or by ATR (attenuated total reflectance). Other methods: fluorimetry (more sensitive and selective than UV — e.g. quinine), atomic absorption spectroscopy (metals such as lead, iron, zinc), NMR (structure elucidation), mass spectrometry (molecular mass and structure; with LC or GC for identification and impurity profiling), and near-infrared and Raman handheld devices for rapid screening of medicines in the field.

topics.title: Chromatographic Methods
topics.summary: TLC, HPLC and GC: principles, parameters, system suitability and applications.

notes.b: Chromatography separates components by differential distribution between a stationary phase and a mobile phase. Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) uses silica gel plates; spots are visualised under UV (254 nm) or with reagents (iodine vapour, ninhydrin for amino acids, Dragendorff's for alkaloids). The retardation factor Rf = distance travelled by the spot ÷ distance travelled by the solvent front (0–1). TLC is cheap and used for identification, limit tests for impurities and screening (e.g. GPHF Minilab kits for detecting substandard and falsified medicines in low-resource settings).
k: Rf = spot distance / solvent front distance

notes.b: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is the most widely used assay technique for drugs. Reversed-phase HPLC (non-polar C18 stationary phase, polar mobile phase such as water–methanol or acetonitrile with buffer) retains non-polar compounds longer; detectors include UV/diode-array, fluorescence and mass spectrometry. Key parameters: retention time (identity), peak area (quantity), resolution (Rs ≥ 1.5 for baseline separation), theoretical plates (efficiency), tailing factor (symmetry, ideally ≤ 2) and repeatability — tested as 'system suitability' before analysis. Gas chromatography (GC) separates volatile, thermally stable compounds (residual solvents, ethanol, essential oils) using an inert carrier gas and detectors such as flame ionisation (FID) or mass spectrometry; derivatisation increases volatility.

topics.title: Method Validation and Pharmacopoeial Quality Tests
topics.summary: ICH validation parameters, and identity, assay, impurity, dissolution and uniformity tests.

notes.b: Analytical methods must be validated to show they are fit for purpose (ICH Q2 guideline). Parameters: specificity/selectivity (measures the analyte without interference from excipients, impurities or degradants), linearity and range, accuracy (closeness to the true value — recovery studies), precision (repeatability, intermediate precision, reproducibility — expressed as %RSD), limit of detection (LOD) and limit of quantitation (LOQ), and robustness (unaffected by small deliberate changes in conditions). Stability-indicating methods separate the drug from its degradation products (tested by forced degradation — acid, base, oxidation, heat, light).
k: Specificity, linearity, accuracy, precision, LOD/LOQ, robustness

notes.b: Pharmacopoeial monographs specify tests: identification; assay (content usually 95–105% of label claim for many tablets — limits vary by monograph); related substances (impurities); uniformity of dosage units (content uniformity or weight variation); disintegration; dissolution (e.g. not less than a stated percentage, Q, released in a set time using basket or paddle apparatus); friability and hardness for tablets; sterility, bacterial endotoxins and particulate matter for injections; pH and microbial limits for non-sterile liquids. Certificates of analysis accompany batches. Stability testing (ICH Q1 — long-term 30 °C/65–75% RH for climatic zone IVa/IVb, which includes Nigeria; accelerated 40 °C/75% RH) establishes shelf life.
k: Nigeria is in climatic zone IV (hot, humid)

topics.title: Substandard and Falsified Medicines
topics.summary: Definitions, public health impact, detection, and regulatory responses in Nigeria.

notes.b: WHO definitions: substandard medicines are authorised products that fail quality standards or specifications (e.g. poor manufacturing, degradation from poor storage in heat and humidity); falsified medicines deliberately or fraudulently misrepresent their identity, composition or source (e.g. no active ingredient, wrong ingredient, fake packaging); unregistered/unlicensed medicines have not been evaluated by the national regulator. They cause treatment failure, antimicrobial resistance (sub-therapeutic antimalarials and antibiotics), adverse effects, death and loss of trust. Antimalarials and antibiotics are among the most frequently affected in sub-Saharan Africa.

Nigeria's NAFDAC has deployed technologies such as Mobile Authentication Service (MAS — scratch-off codes verified by SMS), TruScan handheld Raman spectrometers at ports and markets, and the Greenbook database of registered products; it runs post-marketing surveillance and pharmacovigilance and prosecutes offenders. The late Professor Dora Akunyili, former NAFDAC Director-General, is widely credited with major gains against fake drugs. Pharmacists should buy only from licensed suppliers, check NAFDAC registration numbers, batch numbers, expiry dates and packaging, store medicines correctly, report suspected poor-quality products, and educate the public to avoid open-market drug hawkers. Good distribution practice and cold-chain management protect quality throughout the supply chain.
k: Buy from licensed suppliers; report suspects
